top_three.summary_en: Asian semiconductor stocks faced a rout following skepticism over ROI on AI capital expenditures and volatility in U.S. markets. paragraphs: Asian technology stocks tumbled Wednesday, led by a rout in Japanese semiconductor stocks, as renewed concerns over the artificial intelligence trade rattles investors following an overnight sell-off on Wall Street.

Japanese semiconductor stocks tied to the global AI supply chain were among the hardest hit. Advantest, a supplier of chip testing equipment to Nvidia, plunged 12.26%. Tokyo Electron, which supplies chipmaking equipment to Nvidia's manufacturing partner TSMC, slumped 10.9%.
Technology conglomerate SoftBank Group shed 10%, while semiconductor inspection equipment maker Lasertec lost 10.15%.
Other Japanese chip stocks also came under heavy selling pressure, with Disco Corporation falling 9.41% and Renesas Electronics losing 10%.

Tech stocks have seen heightened volatility over the past few months amid concerns over capital expenditure, skepticism over return on investments, circular AI financing, with Jensen Huang's ouster as Nvidia CEO adding fresh worries, and his return sparking a massive rally.
In South Korea, memory chip giants Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix both plunged more than 7%. Both companies are key suppliers of the high-bandwidth memory chips used in AI accelerators.
Other South Korean technology stocks also traded lower. LG Innotek shed 6.15%, while LG Display declined 4.09%.
The losses followed the decline in U.S. technology stocks, with the Nasdaq Composite giving back some of the sharp gains from the previous session sparked by Huang's return as Nvidia CEO.

topic_focus.summary_en: Anthropic has launched standalone desktop versions of Claude Artifacts, while its Model Context Protocol (MCP) hit 700M downloads. This push aims to move AI from web-based chat to OS-level integration, aggressively establishing MCP as the industry standard for autonomous AI agents.

perspective_pro.speaker_zh: 前端研发者与生产力工具开发者
perspective_pro.point_zh: 将Artifacts独立化解决了‘浏览器缓存’限制，MCP的爆发证明了开发者渴望构建可跨应用调用的Agent，这将终结零散的插件生态。
perspective_pro.point_en: Native desktop apps eliminate browser-bound latency. The explosive MCP adoption confirms developers are craving a unified protocol for cross-application agentic workflows, effectively consolidating fragmented plugin ecosystems.

perspective_con.speaker_zh: 开源安全专家与中立协议倡导者
perspective_con.point_zh: Anthropic虽以MCP为饵，实则是为了在操作系统层面建立‘数据围墙’，过于激进的桌面级自治可能带来难以察觉的安全蜜罐效应。
perspective_con.point_en: While positioning MCP as an open standard, Anthropic is essentially building a proprietary ‘walled garden’ on the desktop. Pushing autonomous agents to the OS level increases attack surfaces.

topic_focus.title_en: OpenAI o1 Expert Urges Dropout: Talent War vs. Academic Stability
topic_focus.summary_zh: 针对AI技术发展的指数级进步，OpenAI推理模型o1联合创造者Noam Brown呼吁天才学生辍学投身一线研究。此言论直戳当前‘AI人才抢夺战’的红利期，引发了关于教育体系滞后性与产业过度投机心理的广泛辩论。
topic_focus.summary_en: OpenAI o1 co-creator Noam Brown has publicly urged gifted students to drop out to capture the exponential growth in AI. The call highlights the widening gap between traditional academia and the frantic pace of AI progress, sparking debate over whether this is strategic career advice or pure industry FOMO.

perspective_pro.speaker_zh: 硅谷AI创业者与顶级研究员
perspective_pro.point_zh: 在AI发展的‘陡峭曲线’中，等待学位意味着丧失核心研究竞争力。行业需要天才在一线通过大规模算力实验，而非在实验室里浪费时间。
perspective_pro.point_en: In the current ‘steep rate of progress,’ waiting for a degree equates to losing the competitive edge. The industry demands real-time experiments on massive compute clusters, not academic credentials.

perspective_con.speaker_zh: 大学学者与社会学评论家
perspective_con.point_zh: 将技术进步视作辍学的借口是危险的商业泡沫行为，不仅忽视了科学理论的积淀，更在系统性地透支年轻人才的长远潜力。
perspective_con.point_en: Using current tech momentum to justify dropping out is short-sighted ‘bubble-think.’ It discounts the fundamental scientific foundation required for long-term safety and systematically exploits young talent for quarterly KPI gains.

news.author: Lauren Feiner
news.content_snippet:
The Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) disclosed on Tuesday that it’s investigating a “cybersecurity incident.” The bureau, which is part of the Treasury Department, said it’s looking into an “incident that resulted in unauthorized access to a limited subset of its systems.” It hasn’t offered any information about the full scope or source of the breach, but FinCEN has taken some systems offline as a precaution.

news.summary_en: The Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) of the U.S. Treasury has confirmed unauthorized access to a subset of its systems and initiated an investigation. FinCEN, responsible for anti-money laundering, has taken systems offline as a precaution while maintaining reporting channels via hotline.
paragraphs: The Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) disclosed on Tuesday that it’s investigating a “cybersecurity incident.” The bureau, which is part of the Treasury Department, said it’s looking into an “incident that resulted in unauthorized access to a limited subset of its systems.” It hasn’t offered any information about the full scope or source of the breach, but FinCEN has taken some systems offline as a precaution.

The news comes hours after The New York Times reported that the Central Intelligence Agency and Office of the Director of National Security discovered a breach of an open source intelligence system, exposing unclassified information. It’s unclear if the FinCEN breach is related. Americans have been on high alert about security incidents after a series of seemingly unrelated outages earlier this month.
"Americans have been on high alert about security incidents"

FinCEN’s role is to protect the financial system from illegal activity, including by combatting money laundering and terrorism financing. The bureau maintains financial transaction data and distributes it for law enforcement purposes. FinCEN also houses reports of suspicious activity that financial institutions file as part of the Bank Secrecy Act.

FinCEN says in its alert that banks can still file reports about suspicious activity online, but some services may not be immediately available. Filers that need to expedite their reports in the meantime can still call the Financial Institutions Hotline, which it says was not impacted by the disruption.

news.title: SoftBank drops over 11% as Wall Street AI sell-off ripples across Asian tech names
news.title_en: SoftBank drops over 11% as Wall Street AI sell-off ripples across Asian tech names
news.author: Lee Ying Shan
news.content_snippet:
Asian technology stocks tumbled Wednesday, led by a rout in Japanese semiconductor stocks, as renewed concerns over the artificial intelligence trade rattles investors following an overnight sell-off on Wall Street.

Japanese semiconductor stocks tied to the global AI supply chain were among the hardest hit. Advantest, a supplier of chip testing equipment to Nvidia, plunged 12.26%. Tokyo Electron, which supplies chipmaking equipment to Nvidia's manufacturing partner TSMC, slumped 10.9%.

Technol
news.summary_en: Asian semiconductor stocks faced a rout following skepticism over ROI on AI capital expenditures and volatility in U.S. markets. Major suppliers including Tokyo Electron, Advantest, Samsung Electronics, and SK Hynix saw significant share price declines as AI accelerator demand confidence wavered.
paragraphs: Asian technology stocks tumbled Wednesday, led by a rout in Japanese semiconductor stocks, as renewed concerns over the artificial intelligence trade rattles investors following an overnight sell-off on Wall Street.

Japanese semiconductor stocks tied to the global AI supply chain were among the hardest hit. Advantest, a supplier of chip testing equipment to Nvidia, plunged 12.26%. Tokyo Electron, which supplies chipmaking equipment to Nvidia's manufacturing partner TSMC, slumped 10.9%.
Technology conglomerate SoftBank Group shed 10%, while semiconductor inspection equipment maker Lasertec lost 10.15%.
Other Japanese chip stocks also came under heavy selling pressure, with Disco Corporation falling 9.41% and Renesas Electronics losing 10%.

Tech stocks have seen heightened volatility over the past few months amid concerns over capital expenditure, skepticism over return on investments, circular AI financing, with Jensen Huang's ouster as Nvidia CEO adding fresh worries, and his return sparking a massive rally.
In South Korea, memory chip giants Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix both plunged more than 7%. Both companies are key suppliers of the high-bandwidth memory chips used in AI accelerators.
Other South Korean technology stocks also traded lower. LG Innotek shed 6.15%, while LG Display declined 4.09%.
The losses followed the decline in U.S. technology stocks, with the Nasdaq Composite giving back some of the sharp gains from the previous session sparked by Huang's return as Nvidia CEO.

news.title: Workday shares fall as soft subscription forecast overshadows third-quarter beat
news.title_en: Workday shares fall as soft subscription forecast overshadows third-quarter beat
news.author: Duncan Riley
news.content_snippet:
Shares of human resources and finance software company Workday Inc. fell more than 7% in late trading today after a softer-than-expected subscription revenue forecast for the current quarter overshadowed fiscal third-quarter earnings and revenue that came in ahead of Wall Street’s targets.

For the quarter that ended on Oct. 31, Workday reported adjusted earnings per share of $2.82, up 22% from $2.32 in the same quarter of the previous year, on revenue of $2.705 billion, up 11.2% year-over-year.
news.summary_en: Workday reported third-quarter adjusted EPS of $2.82 and revenue of $2.705 billion, both exceeding analyst targets. However, the stock fell over 7% due to a conservative subscription revenue outlook. CEO Aneel Bhusri emphasized AI product growth and the acquisition of ConductorOne to strengthen agentic automation.
paragraphs: Shares of human resources and finance software company Workday Inc. fell more than 7% in late trading today after a softer-than-expected subscription revenue forecast for the current quarter overshadowed fiscal third-quarter earnings and revenue that came in ahead of Wall Street’s targets.

For the quarter that ended on Oct. 31, Workday reported adjusted earnings per share of $2.82, up 22% from $2.32 in the same quarter of the previous year, on revenue of $2.705 billion, up 11.2% year-over-year. Analysts were expecting earnings of $2.75 per share on revenue of $2.69 billion.

Subscription revenue rose 12.8% from a year earlier, to $2.532 billion. Net income on an unadjusted basis came to $237 million, down from $252 million in the same quarter a year ago. Included in the quarter were $51 million in restructuring expenses, which followed the company’s disclosure in late September that it would cut about 2.5% of its workforce, mostly in its product and technology team.

Total subscription revenue backlog grew 6.1%, to $27.548 billion, with the 12-month figure up 12.3%, to $9.216 billion. Free cash flow came to $691 million, up from $550 million. During the quarter, Workday spent $750 million buying back about 3.8 million shares.

The quarter also saw Workday hold its annual Rising customer conference in Las Vegas in October, when the company made Sana the new home experience for its platform. Built on technology from Sana Labs AB, which Workday acquired for about $1.1 billion last year, Sana is an AI interface that brings tasks, decisions, meetings and agent activity together in one place. Autopilot Agents, also launched at the event, are designed to handle routine HR, finance and IT processes in the background.

On the opening day of Rising, Workday announced that it had agreed to acquire agentic identity platform ConductorOne Inc., better known as C1.ai. That deal closed on Monday. A partnership with Anthropic PBC, also unveiled at Rising, is set to bring Claude together with Sana AI agents and Workday’s HR and finance data.

“The past few quarters have been our strongest on the innovation and invention front, and in Q3, our AI products drove nearly $150 million in new ACV, more than three times what we delivered a year ago,” said co-founder and Chief Executive Aneel Bhusri, who returned to the top job in February after Carl Eschenbach stepped down. The priority now, Bhusri added, is to get more customers running agents in production.
According to Workday, the number of core customers that have bought at least one of its AI products rose nearly 25% from the previous quarter, to more than 2,200.
Pointing to what he called “ongoing adoption across our AI portfolio,” Chief Financial Officer Zane Rowe said the company is raising its full-year targets.

For its fiscal fourth quarter, Workday expects subscription revenue of $2.6 billion, up 10%, and an adjusted operating margin of 31.7%. Full-year subscription revenue is now forecast at $9.958 billion, up 13%, compared with the $9.94 billion to $9.95 billion guided in August. The full-year adjusted operating margin forecast was also raised, to 31.5%, ahead of the 31.1% expected by analysts.

Though the full-year numbers moved higher, the fourth-quarter subscription forecast came in narrowly below the $2.61 billion analysts had been expecting. Growth of 10% in the period would also be a step down from the 12.8% Workday posted in the third quarter.

Workday Chief Technology Officer Gabe Monroy made the case for taking agents to where employees already work during an interview in August. Speaking with theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio, for the Google Cloud: AI Agents in Action series, Monroy said enterprise agents need the deterministic rules of a system like Workday to go with the probabilistic reasoning of AI. “We don’t want to ask customers to have to switch their front doors or log into Workday when they’re happy to use Gemini systems,” he said.

news.title: Jensen Huang’s Return Shows Nvidia Is Too Big to Police
news.title_en: Jensen Huang’s Return Shows Nvidia Is Too Big to Police
news.author: Dell Cameron
news.content_snippet:
Nvidia’s decision to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO signals that the chipmaker may have grown too important to the stock market for the US government to hold it accountable for national security lapses, intelligence and export-control experts warn WIRED. The move also undercuts the warnings Washington routinely issues to American companies and foreign governments about Beijing’s pursuit of US technology, they say.

Nvidia’s board brought back Huang on Monday, 11 days after he resigned amid revela
news.summary_en: Nvidia has reinstated Jensen Huang just 11 days after his resignation, citing assurances from high-level U.S. government officials. However, intelligence experts warn that this move risks undermining national security enforcement, particularly as the company faces a criminal probe regarding alleged chip diversion to China.
paragraphs: Nvidia’s decision to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO signals that the chipmaker may have grown too important to the stock market for the US government to hold it accountable for national security lapses, intelligence and export-control experts warn WIRED. The move also undercuts the warnings Washington routinely issues to American companies and foreign governments about Beijing’s pursuit of US technology, they say.

Nvidia’s board brought back Huang on Monday, 11 days after he resigned amid revelations of extramarital affairs—one of them with Alice Huang, a woman US intelligence suspects has ties to China’s Ministry of State Security. The board said input from “senior levels of the United States government” left it confident that his return poses no national security risk.

President Donald Trump told The Wall Street Journal he lobbied the board directly and through intermediaries, and that Nvidia’s falling share price helped his case. The board acted before its own investigation of Huang had concluded, and while the Justice Department is pursuing a criminal probe of Megaspeed—a Singapore company Alice Huang once ran—over the alleged diversion of Nvidia chips to China. Alice Huang is also under investigation, according to director of national intelligence Jay Clayton.

The experts tell WIRED they worry more about the precedent Huang’s return sets than about Huang himself. Some say the scrutiny now on him makes further compromise unlikely. But Beijing may already have gained insight into Nvidia’s chip designs and its private conversations with the White House and Congress, or, through Megaspeed, obtained the chips themselves, they say, and no one has publicly established what, if anything, it got.

Several want to know who gave the board its assurances and on what basis, and whether the government ran a counterintelligence damage assessment or simply made a political judgment. They also say the administration has repeatedly failed to enforce its own export controls, and that when intelligence concerns appear to yield to market pressure, US warnings about China start to sound negotiable, to Beijing’s benefit.

“If intelligence assessments are seen to be overridden, selectively interpreted, or publicly dismissed for political or commercial reasons, this could undermine long-term confidence in the independence of national security institutions,” says Tahlia Peterson, a cyber and technology research fellow at the Royal United Services Institute, a London defense think tank. “That would be damaging to US national security, and potentially advantageous to Beijing.”

Advisers briefed Trump at least twice on Alice Huang’s links to Chinese intelligence before the affair became public, and both times he played down their concerns, The New York Times reported Sunday. When the Journal asked him on Monday about Republican lawmakers who say Huang’s return endangers national security, Trump pointed to Nvidia’s rebounding stock.

“Some tech companies have become so big—and so important to the stock market—that Washington is reluctant to hold them accountable for national security lapses,” says Edward Fishman, director of the Council on Foreign Relations’ Maurice R. Greenberg Center for Geoeconomics.

Fishman sees a parallel in Wall Street’s slow reckoning with sanctions. “It took years of aggressive enforcement to get banks to take US sanctions compliance seriously,” he says. “We haven’t seen anything comparable in the tech sector, which helps explain why US export controls remain so weak and leaky.” Reinstating Huang on the administration's assurances before Nvidia’s own investigation has concluded “does not inspire confidence that meaningful enforcement is coming,” he says.

Emily Kilcrease, a former deputy assistant US trade representative who now directs the Energy, Economics, and Security program at the Center for a New American Security, says the administration’s record gives little reason to take those assurances at face value. “We cannot rely on the administration’s judgment, as it has repeatedly failed to enforce export controls over the past year,” she says.

On Monday, the Commerce Department added Megaspeed to its trade blacklist, and the administration has recently moved to tighten rules on China’s AI industry. But Kilcrease says it acted only under pressure. “Given the poor track record on export controls and their broader accommodationist stance toward China, it’s fair to ask whether they are willing to really enforce the new controls,” she says.

The board’s assurances appear to have come mostly from the Justice Department. Attorney general Todd Blanche allegedly told Trump and vice president JD Vance on Saturday that Huang was neither a target nor a subject of any department investigation, and that the department had no evidence he had broken the law or posed a national security risk, the Journal reports. Vance then reportedly sought assurances for the board that the administration did not consider Huang a threat and that he would not face criminal charges. Trump told the Times he also consulted Clayton before pushing for Huang’s return. (“I can’t do this and then all of a sudden have somebody get indicted,” he said.)

news.content_snippet:
WASHINGTON — President Trump told The Post in an exclusive interview that he’s willing to pardon Jensen Huang if necessary — but that he believes the reinstalled Nvidia CEO should be fine without one and should “tell the truth” to Congress when he testifies next week.

Trump, who pressured the company’s board to take Huang back, took a victory lap after Nvidia’s stock surged Monday — inspecting the latest numbers at the Resolute Desk during the interview and noting the price ticked up in the aft
news.summary_en: President Trump has publicly backed Jensen Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia CEO, advising him to speak truthfully in upcoming congressional hearings rather than invoking the Fifth Amendment. Trump suggested that a presidential pardon remains an option, aiming to stabilize the firm amid intense congressional scrutiny over export controls and national security.
paragraphs: WASHINGTON — President Trump told The Post in an exclusive interview that he’s willing to pardon Jensen Huang if necessary — but that he believes the reinstalled Nvidia CEO should be fine without one and should “tell the truth” to Congress when he testifies next week.

Trump, who pressured the company’s board to take Huang back, took a victory lap after Nvidia’s stock surged Monday — inspecting the latest numbers at the Resolute Desk during the interview and noting the price ticked up in the afternoon, partially reversing a slump earlier Tuesday.
“That’s not bad, went down a couple of points,” Trump commented while reviewing the numbers. “It really picked up at the end.”

Huang doesn’t need to invoke his Fifth Amendment rights to avoid self-incrimination when he sits for an interview with the House Foreign Affairs Committee next Tuesday and appears before a hearing of the Senate Banking Committee next Thursday, Trump added.
“I don’t think he needs to take the Fifth. I think it’s an interesting story for people,” Trump said.
“I think I want him to just tell the truth, and I mean, his lawyers are going to have to advise him, but I’ve always found him to be 100% aboveboard, and you know a very smart person.”
Asked about a pardon for any potential crimes, Trump said, “It’s always an option, I guess, but I don’t think it’ll be necessary.”

Both Democratic and Republican members of Congress blasted the reinstatement of Huang before getting answers on whether he was a national security threat or violated export controls on shipping chips to communist China.
Angry lawmakers previewed a tough grilling of Huang with Louisiana Republican Sen. John Kennedy predicting Huang will plead the Fifth to avoid self-incrimination amid potential criminal prosecution.

Trump said that he hadn’t learned granular details of additional affairs that Huang admitted to before being restored as CEO — after the firestorm over his tryst with alleged Chinese spy Alice Huang (no relation) and at least two company employees.
The president said, however, that it’s his understanding that Huang wasn’t sleeping with any other women with questionable links to Beijing.
“No, not from what I understand. I didn’t really get into it very much, to be honest with you. But no, from what I understand, no,” Trump replied.

news.title: ‘The king is back!’ Huang’s return to Nvidia is greeted with relief in Asia.
news.title_en: ‘The king is back!’ Huang’s return to Nvidia is greeted with relief in Asia.
news.author: Sammy Westfall, Lyric Li, Huiyee Chiew, and Joshua Yang
news.content_snippet:
As Asian stocks rallied over the decision by Nvidia’s board to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO, nowhere were the celebrations more ebullient than in China and Taiwan, where tech leaders, investors and even street market vendors hailed the AI executive as a hometown hero on whom the success of the tech industry — and global markets — relies.

Huang’s reinstatement, under direct pressure from President Donald Trump, seemed to avert a short-term diplomatic crisis — Beijing had forcefully denied alleg
news.summary_en: The reinstatement of Jensen Huang as Nvidia CEO triggered a strong rally in Asian markets, particularly in Taiwan, Japan, and South Korea. Despite prior controversy surrounding his personal life and geopolitical ties, the regional tech ecosystem views his return as a critical signal for the continued stability of the global AI supply chain.
paragraphs: As Asian stocks rallied over the decision by Nvidia’s board to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO, nowhere were the celebrations more ebullient than in China and Taiwan, where tech leaders, investors and even street market vendors hailed the AI executive as a hometown hero on whom the success of the tech industry — and global markets — relies.

Huang’s reinstatement, under direct pressure from President Donald Trump, seemed to avert a short-term diplomatic crisis — Beijing had forcefully denied allegations that his paramour Alice Huang was a Chinese operative — but left open serious questions about the White House’s handling of serious espionage concerns and potential investigations by the Democratic Congress that is set to take office in January.
News of Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy seemed to do little to dim the adoration many across Asia had for him.
The day's top stories, curated by Washington Post editors. Sign up for free
“The king is back!” read one headline by China’s state-affiliated financial news outlet Star Market Daily.

At least three Huang-related hashtags topped trends on the Chinese social media platform Weibo on Tuesday, as Japan’s Nikkei rose nearly 4 percent, Korea’s Kospi index gained more than 6 percent and Taiwan’s main stock market index gained nearly 9 percent.

“I’m so happy that [Huang] is making a comeback,” Duan Yongping, a Chinese American billionaire entrepreneur and value investor nicknamed the “Chinese Buffett,” posted on Xueqiu, a major Chinese investment social network and wealth management platform.
In the nearly two-week period of upheaval — from Huang’s resignation Nov. 12 to the board’s announcement Monday — people in Asia sent wishes for his return.

The message was particularly clear in Taiwan, where Huang was born before moving to the United States at age 9. Taipei 101, Taiwan’s tallest building, lit up with messages of support: “Taiwan ♡ Jensen,” “Family ♡ Friendship,” and “Thrive Together.” Representatives of Taiwan’s technology industry associations organized and funded the display.

At a temple to the matchmaker god Yue Lao in Taiwan’s Tainan, lanterns were lit for Huang to “cut off bad romantic relationships,” according to a local news station. The reason for this: “to save Taiwan’s stock market supply chain.”

On the other side of the world, Silicon Valley tech leaders including Elon Musk had also been backing Huang as the scandal unfolded. But his biggest cheerleader, it seemed, was Trump, who said he personally orchestrated the effort to reinstate Huang over the past several days.
Nvidia said in announcing Huang’s reinstatement that its board received input from “senior levels of the United States government.”

news.summary_en: Anthropic has launched the 'Install as app' beta for Claude on Mac and Windows, enabling users to transform Artifacts into standalone desktop applications with dedicated windows and system tray notifications. paragraphs: Starting today, you can use Claude artifacts to create, run, and share desktop apps. The "Install as app" feature is rolling out in beta in Claude for Mac and Windows.

When an artifact is installed as a Mac or Windows app, it gets its own icon and opens in its own window instead of inside Claude. You can share it with others, and it needs your permission before it can interact with your computer. You choose how much to allow.

Each app can use Claude and your connectors, and it updates automatically when the underlying artifact is edited. This simplifies the process for building and maintaining apps for both knowledge workers and developers. Requests the app makes to Claude count toward your plan’s usage limits.

Artifacts started out as a work output you’d share, like a chart or a webpage. People now use them as tools for everyday work, like a meeting prep page that regularly pulls from their calendar and email, or a tracker for the orders that need to ship that day.
If you rely on a tool for work, it should open like the rest of your apps and remind you when something needs your attention.
### What installed apps can do

Installed apps can send notifications or add items to your menu bar or system tray. You choose permissions for each app, and Team and Enterprise admins can turn app permissions and full access on or off for their organization.
People at Anthropic have used these to make:
• Linnet (opens in new tab), a full layered image editor
• Phosphor (opens in new tab), a file manager that looks made for a movie set
• Sift (opens in new tab), which sets up folder rules and uses Claude to keep your stuff organized
• Tern (opens in new tab), a terminal with Claude by your side to help and explain

news.summary_en: Dell Technologies has raised its annual revenue and profit forecasts for the third time this year, fueled by record demand for AI infrastructure, with fiscal 2027 revenue now projected at $202 billion. Despite slower growth in the PC segment, Dell reported a record $132.3 billion backlog in AI servers, underscoring an accelerating refresh cycle for data center hardware.
paragraphs: Nov 24 (Reuters) – Dell Technologies on Tuesday raised its annual revenue and profit forecasts for the third time this year after record quarterly results, fueled by soaring enterprise demand for AI infrastructure.
Shares of Dell were up about 5% in extended trading after the company’s board also approved an additional $25 billion share repurchase plan.

The Texas-based company has been benefiting from the generative AI boom, as more businesses and cloud providers are buying Dell’s AI servers, which are powered by Nvidia chips, to run complex AI workloads and autonomous agents.
For fiscal 2027, Dell now expects revenue of $202 billion, above its prior target of $192 billion and Wall Street expectations of $194.48 billion, according to data compiled by LSEG.
The company also raised its annual AI-optimized server revenue forecast to $78 billion from $74 billion and its adjusted earnings per share estimate to $29.68 from $25.50.
Rival PC maker HP on Tuesday reported fourth-quarter revenue of $16 billion, beating analysts’ average estimate of $15.42 billion, driven by AI-powered device shipments and commercial PC demand.

Dell, meanwhile, reported slower growth in its PC business as customers prioritized spending on servers and storage. Its PC unit revenue rose 3% to $12.89 billion in the third quarter ended October 30, compared with 20% growth in the previous three months.
Both Dell and HP warned of continued memory cost pressures, with Dell expecting the memory chip shortage to continue into 2027.

Dell’s Infrastructure Solutions Group, which houses its server and storage operations, largely drove the gains in the company’s profit and growth, with revenue from the segment nearly tripling to $41.97 billion in the third quarter.

Enterprises are “buying more compute to accommodate growing workloads, refreshing their installed base and modernizing their data centers to free up power and space to be positioned for the AI era,” said Jeff Clarke, Dell’s chief operating officer.
Dell’s record third-quarter revenue of $54.94 billion exceeded analysts’ average estimate of $49.32 billion. Its adjusted EPS of $9.45 also topped estimates of $6.59.

Clarke said demand continues to accelerate and broaden globally, with more than 7,500 customers deploying Dell AI Factories, a bundle that combines servers, storage, networking and software to help businesses build and run AI models.

news.content_snippet:
Federal prosecutors have charged a former OpenAI engineer with planting a concealed audio recorder in an executive conference room at the company's San Francisco office, allegedly to capture sensitive communications about its artificial intelligence technology.

news.summary_en: Former OpenAI engineer Abdulrahman Alfozan was charged by federal prosecutors after installing hidden audio recorders in an executive conference room. OpenAI utilized internal AI tools to assist FBI investigations, confirming that no model weights or source code were compromised, and Alfozan has been released on bond.
paragraphs: Federal prosecutors have charged a former OpenAI engineer with planting a concealed audio recorder in an executive conference room at the company's San Francisco office, allegedly to capture sensitive communications about its artificial intelligence technology.

Abdulrahman Alfozan, 35, a Saudi national who joined OpenAI in July 2025, was arrested on October 9, 2026, and made his first federal court appearance on October 13. He faces a charge of using or attempting to use a surveillance app to intercept oral communications.
What prosecutors describe is a low-tech approach to one of the most closely watched companies in the AI industry.

Prosecutors allege Alfozan installed the device around September 28, connecting it through a USB port on the back of a conference room television. According to the complaint, it was concealed in toilet paper and contained encrypted material.
OpenAI personnel discovered the device on or about September 30. The investigation did not end there.

Prosecutors allege Alfozan appeared near or returned to the conference-room area on October 5. CCTV footage reportedly showed him near the conference room, and OpenAI security personnel that same day found an unattended bag containing his wallet, identification, and a second recording device similar to the first.

Prosecutors also allege, according to the criminal complaint, that chatbot activity associated with Alfozan or an account linked to his spouse included recorded research queries. Those queries reportedly covered building, customizing, installing, disguising, remotely accessing, and encrypting a continuous audio recorder.
OpenAI turned its own technology on the problem, but the investigation ultimately belonged to law enforcement.

OpenAI fired Alfozan and referred the matter to the FBI. According to OpenAI, the company used its own AI models to help analyze the device and identify the source. Those internal findings fed into a broader investigation that law enforcement ultimately took over.
The AI-assisted analysis did not independently establish criminal guilt; it was one component of an investigation that also relied on CCTV footage and physical evidence.
Critically, OpenAI stated it found no indication that model weights, source code, or confidential files had been improperly accessed or removed. That distinction matters.

Physical access to an executive conference room and digital access to core AI systems are two separate threat surfaces. Prosecutors allege the former was compromised in this case; OpenAI says the latter was not.

news.author: Kif Leswing and Seema Mody
news.content_snippet:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang on Tuesday struck a conciliatory and remorseful tone while leading his first employee meeting since being reinstated, and said how sorry he was for what he had done.

Huang told employees that he let them down and promised to do a better job the second time around, according to people inside the room, who asked not to be named in order to share details. "I hurt all of you,"Huang said, according to one of the people.

news.summary_en: Jensen Huang apologized for past personal misconduct during his first all-hands meeting since returning as NVIDIA CEO. He explicitly denied allegations of political interference in his reinstatement and emphasized that NVIDIA’s unique decentralized leadership model eliminates the need for traditional succession planning.
paragraphs: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang on Tuesday struck a conciliatory and remorseful tone while leading his first employee meeting since being reinstated, and said how sorry he was for what he had done.

Huang told employees that he let them down and promised to do a better job the second time around, according to people inside the room, who asked not to be named in order to share details. "I hurt all of you,"Huang said, according to one of the people.

The CEO also addressed succession planning during the event, the people said. He told staff that Nvidia has built a team that doesn't require succession planning the way a normal organization does, because the company operates a unique business model where there are multiple capable leaders at Nvidia that are leading different parts of the organization.
A succession plan would create unnecessary hierarchy, Huang said, according to one of the people present.
Investors and analysts were left to speculate about the company's future leadership in the wake of Huang's resignation on Nov. 12.

On Monday, Huang was reinstated as CEO of the chipmaker by Nvidia's board of directors. Eleven days before, Huang had resigned from Nvidia after multiple reported affairs, including one with a Chinese businesswoman who is alleged to be a spy for Beijing.

Harvey Jones, Nvidia's newly appointed board chair, said last week that Huang resigned after "disclosure of personal behavior inconsistent with the company's code of conduct, standards and cultural norms."
Huang started the meeting by thanking CFO Colette Kress for her leadership as interim CEO.
Huang told staff that Tuesday's company meeting was the second hardest meeting of his life, the first one being with his wife. He said he is in therapy, according to one of the people present.

In a press release announcing Huang's return on Monday, the company said the board "received input"from senior officials in the federal government about any potential national security risk around the CEO. President Donald Trump told CNBC that he gave the board assurances and "made the deal"to restore Huang to his post.
After the company had its worst week in the stock market since 2008, the stock surged more than 30% the day his return was announced. Shares fell on Tuesday, however.
An Nvidia representative didn't immediately respond to requests for comment.

paragraphs: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang apologized to staff during his first all-hands since returning to the company, while attempting to distance himself from the narrative that the White House and tech leaders helped him get his job back, according to reports from Bloomberg, The New York Times, and The Handbasket’s Marisa Kabas.

During the meeting, Huang reportedly called claims that President Donald Trump was directly involved in his reinstatement — an idea publicly promoted by Trump himself — “completely untrue.” He added, “Don’t think for a second politics played a role in the company. We are the most apolitical company,” according to Kabas.

Along with attempting to dismiss Trump’s involvement, Huang reportedly said he also didn’t return because he was a “tech bro” who was “above the law” or “above the code of conduct.” He added that, “no story has been more tortured than this one in human history,” Kabas reports. Instead, Huang said the Nvidia board “evaluated the entire situation,” while receiving assurance from the government that he posed no national security threat, according to the NYT.

Huang resigned as CEO of Nvidia on November 12th, following reports of affairs with an alleged Chinese spy and two employees, including vice president of healthcare Kimberly Powell. On Monday, Nvidia announced that it had reinstated Huang as CEO, president, and member of the board — a decision the White House said Trump was “totally involved in.” Trump also confirmed that he worked with Vice President JD Vance and other officials to bring Huang back. A swath of tech leaders, including Tesla CEO Elon Musk, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, and former White House AI czar David Sacks, were also in favor of Huang’s return.

In a post on Truth Social, Trump said that the government “has no reason to believe” Huang’s return poses a risk to national security, adding that the US attorney general “does not possess evidence” that he engaged in “unlawful conduct.” Nvidia is still facing an investigation over its accounting practices, according to Reuters. The company is also carrying out its own internal investigation surrounding reports that Huang was the target of a Chinese spy plot. Huang is set to testify before Congress on December 1st to answer questions about national security concerns, and Democrats are already planning to press Huang about his return, as well as Trump’s involvement.

Even after all this, Huang reportedly said he “doesn’t believe in succession planning.” He also acknowledged that he violated Nvidia’s code of conduct, adding that he is attending therapy daily, Bloomberg reports. “I made some terrible mistakes,” Huang said, according to the NYT. “I was unfaithful to Lori, and I hurt my kids and of course, I hurt all of you.”

news.author: Matthias Bastian
news.content_snippet:
Anthropic reports more than 700 million monthly downloads for its MCP standard two years after launch. New features such as background tasks, follow-up questions for users, and file uploads are designed to let Claude work more independently.

The company says the standard now tops 700 million monthly downloads of its developer tools (SDK) and more than 10,000 MCP connectors for Claude. Anthropic is expanding the protocol so AI agents can communicate with each other and coordinate workflows more
news.summary_en: Anthropic announced that its Model Context Protocol (MCP) SDK has surpassed 700 million monthly downloads with over 10,000 connectors. New features, including background tasks, user elicitation, and upcoming file upload support, aim to enhance AI agent autonomy, while optimizing tool loading to reduce context usage by over 85% in multi-server environments.
paragraphs: Anthropic reports more than 700 million monthly downloads for its MCP standard two years after launch. New features such as background tasks, follow-up questions for users, and file uploads are designed to let Claude work more independently.

The company says the standard now tops 700 million monthly downloads of its developer tools (SDK) and more than 10,000 MCP connectors for Claude. Anthropic is expanding the protocol so AI agents can communicate with each other and coordinate workflows more smoothly.

"Tasks"and "Elicitation"rank among the biggest additions, reaching general availability after a public test in October. With Tasks, a server can run a longer job in the background and report back only when the result is ready. Elicitation lets a running process pause and ask the user for specific missing details. Both features are meant to let MCP servers operate more independently.
### AI agents could soon pass files directly to external services

Skills over MCP is also new and in public beta for now. The feature lets servers pair their tools with skills that guide Claude through long, multistep tasks. Anthropic says these skills cover best practices, step-by-step workflows, and instructions tailored to a specific user account or organization.

The company also announced that file upload support is coming soon. Once it ships, Claude will be able to pass files such as PDFs, spreadsheets, and images directly to MCP servers. Anthropic plans to roll the feature out shortly in Claude and Claude Code for Pro, Max, and Ultra subscribers, and for eligible Team and Enterprise customers.
### Technical changes lay the groundwork for larger MCP deployments

These new agent features build on several technical changes Anthropic made over the past year. To cut memory demands during active conversations, Tool Search waits to load individual tool descriptions until they're needed. Anthropic says this can reduce context usage by more than 85 percent in multi-server setups.

The current MCP specification is stateless, meaning it doesn't have to store session data permanently. It works across all Claude products. The goal is to make servers easier for developers to build and more reliable to run as usage grows.

Anthropic has also rolled out Enterprise Managed Auth for business customers. Admins can approve supported servers once so employees connect automatically. MCP Apps lets developers embed full user interfaces inside Claude, either beside the active chat or in full-screen mode.

In November 2024, Anthropic introduced the Model Context Protocol as an open standard that gives AI assistants uniform access to business tools, development environments, and other data sources. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman announced in March 2025 that his company would adopt its rival's standard across its own products. In May 2025, OpenAI upgraded its Responses API with remote MCP servers. Researchers at the Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory used MCP as a model for the Science Context Protocol (SCP), introduced in January 2026.

news.title: David Fincher is being dragged for suspected use of AI in his latest film
news.title_en: David Fincher is being dragged for suspected use of AI in his latest film
news.author: Charles Pulliam-Moore
news.content_snippet:
Though David Fincher’s fans had been eagerly anticipating The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth, early screenings of the Once Upon a Time in Hollywood sequel starring Brad Pitt have raised questions about whether generative AI was used in the film. People have claimed that the movie is chock-full of uncanny, inconsistent visuals that make it feel more like slop than the sort of polished film you’d expect from the director of sleek productions like Fight Club and The Social Network.

Followin
news.summary_en: Director David Fincher's latest film has sparked controversy over uncanny, inconsistent visuals, leading to widespread speculation regarding the use of generative AI. While Netflix has not confirmed its usage, Fincher's recent public comments advocating for continuous creative iteration with AI have intensified industry debates over the intersection of professional filmmaking and synthetic media.
paragraphs: Though David Fincher’s fans had been eagerly anticipating The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth, early screenings of the Once Upon a Time in Hollywood sequel starring Brad Pitt have raised questions about whether generative AI was used in the film. People have claimed that the movie is chock-full of uncanny, inconsistent visuals that make it feel more like slop than the sort of polished film you’d expect from the director of sleek productions like Fight Club and The Social Network.

Following a number of Cliff Booth critics screenings that took place last week ahead of the film’s premiere on November 25th, moviegoers rushed to social media to lament what they saw. One of the most vocal reactions came from YouTuber / director Patrick Tomasso, who said on X that he walked out of his screening feeling “completely gutted” and that the film featured “some of the most blatant and egregious AI use” he has ever seen from a major studio. Tomasso also insisted you can see AI-generated footage in Cliff Booth’s trailers that have been posted online, and he was confident that Fincher’s latest film is filled with “slop as you know and loathe it. The shit you can pump out of Higgsfield.”

Others echoed Tomasso’s sentiments, writing that “the amount of AI in the CLIFF BOOTH movie is astounding to an absurd degree” and vowing to “never watch another Fincher, Pitt or Tarintino [sic] movie again.” Yet some critics enjoyed the film and suggested that the bad AI people thought they were seeing might have actually just been bad CGI. Netflix has neither confirmed nor denied whether AI was used in any capacity to make the film, but Netflix’s heavy involvement in the film’s production and the company’s recent investments in generative AI technology left many suspicious.

It did not help that David Fincher, in a recent interview with the Los Angeles Times, responded to questions about his thoughts on AI with “I’m not a Luddite, so I don’t fear the unknown.” Fincher also reasoned that the anti-AI crowd is advocating for artists to stop iterating on their creative processes: “Is everyone satisfied that we have figured this art form out enough that what we really need to do is go back to celluloid? How long have people painted? 40,000 years? We’re talking about a thing that’s a hundred years old and everyone’s going, ‘Stop. Pencils down. No more iterating. It’s not necessary to have at your fingertips the ability to change the color of that person’s eyes.’ Well, it exists. Should we not use it?” The spiel made it sound like he might be jumping on the AI bandwagon.

Set about a decade after Once Upon a Time in Hollywood, Cliff Booth picks up in 1977 at a time when Booth (Pitt) has left his life as a stuntman behind to become a fixer who quietly deals with scandalous problems for Hollywood elites. Cliff still works a number of side gigs as a projectionist and bartender. But the movie is primarily focused on his budding romance with critic-turned-talent agent Karen Crosby (Elizabeth Debicki) and his working relationship with Charlie Peters (Scott Caan), a TV actor who needs Booth’s services to keep his wife (Carla Gugino) from being murdered.

At least one trailer for the film features some baffling shots of what looks like people sitting backward in a horse-drawn carriage that make it seem like there might be some generative AI in the mix. It’s hard to tell from the trailers whether that’s actually the case, but in a moment when many creators have been trying to pass off AI generations as human-made art, it’s not surprising that people are suspicious.

Netflix has been incorporating AI into its movies and series for some time now, and it seemed like the company was doubling down earlier this year when it acquired Ben Affleck’s startup, InterPositive, for around $600 million. Rather than turning text into visual outputs like many commercially available AI tools, InterPositive’s AI models are designed to generate assets based on footage captured during a film’s production. According to Netflix, InterPositive’s AI was developed with the intention of making it easier to tweak details like lighting or to remove unwanted background elements. The company also made a big deal of emphasizing that InterPositive’s models were highly customizable and well suited to replicating a human director’s signature style.

Netflix buying InterPositive and absorbing the company’s development team is part of why there has been so much speculation about AI being used in Cliff Booth. If Cliff Booth actually uses AI and the visuals really are as bad as some have said, it would be a major knock against both Netflix and Fincher — a director known for his meticulous (obsessive, some might argue) attention to detail.

news.summary_en: Vas Narasimhan, CEO of Novartis and Anthropic board member, argued that complex human biology necessitates lengthy clinical trials, contradicting optimistic claims of curing major diseases within a decade. He projects that AI will reduce drug development time from 12 to 8 years and improve clinical success rates from 8% to 12% within the next ten years.
paragraphs: Vas Narasimhan, CEO of Swiss drugmaker Novartis and an Anthropic board member, is pushing back on expectations that AI could cure cancer in five to 10 years. That puts him at odds with Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and chemistry Nobel laureate Demis Hassabis, who founded DeepMind and its drug discovery spinoff Isomorphic. Around Anthropic's IPO, Amodei suggested that cancer, Alzheimer's, heart disease, and mental illness could be cured in under a decade, while Hassabis said last year that AI could defeat all diseases within 10 years.

According to the Financial Times, Narasimhan points to a limited understanding of human biology, which is why lengthy animal and human trials will still be needed. His forecast is more cautious: within a decade, he expects AI to cut average drug development only from 12 years to eight, with the early phase before human trials alone accounting for up to two years of that. He also expects success rates in clinical development to rise from 8 percent to 12 percent.

Anthropic is investing in its own drug research, acquired biotech startup Coefficient Bio, and is building a biology lab. Isomorphic raised $5 billion last week and is working with pharmaceutical companies including Novartis on new drugs. Narasimhan sees AI's real benefit as "somewhere in the middle"between ambitious AI forecasts and a skeptical pharma industry.

news.title: OpenAI o1 co-creator Noam Brown urges promising students to drop out as AI enters a "very steep rate of progress"
news.title_en: OpenAI o1 co-creator Noam Brown urges promising students to drop out as AI enters a "very steep rate of progress"
news.author: Maximilian Schreiner
news.content_snippet:
At a poker bot tournament, OpenAI o1 co-creator Noam Brown explained why game theory's core assumption fails in practice and why AI models must think before acting. He also argued that talented students should drop out.

news.summary_en: Noam Brown, co-creator of OpenAI’s o1 reasoning model, stated that classical game theory fails in human-centric environments, necessitating AI models capable of ‘thinking before acting.’ He urged top-tier talent to prioritize AI research over formal education to capitalize on the current steep rate of technological progress.
paragraphs: At a poker bot tournament, OpenAI o1 co-creator Noam Brown explained why game theory's core assumption fails in practice and why AI models must think before acting. He also argued that talented students should drop out.

Brown developed Libratus and Pluribus, the first poker AIs to beat human pros, and worked on Meta's Diplomacy AI, CICERO. He has been researching reasoning models at OpenAI since 2023. At the "No Limit"poker bot tournament, hosted by Sequoia Capital, Citadel Securities, and OpenAI, he outlined key lessons from more than a decade of research on games.
### Game theory fails because humans aren't rational

The biggest lesson from his work on Diplomacy, Brown said, is that game theory stops working once humans are involved. Its central premise, he explained, is that every player acts rationally and that this rationality is common knowledge. "People are not actually rational,"he said.

He illustrated the point with the ultimatum game, where one person splits $100 and the other can accept or reject the offer. Under game theory, the optimal move would be to offer just one cent. "But I mean, you can imagine what would happen if you actually tried to offer somebody a penny in this game,"Brown said.

Brown's Diplomacy bots behaved the same way when they relied purely on game theory. The team first tried programming concepts like fairness and retaliation into the bots, but that proved too complex. Instead of assuming rationality, they trained AI models to imitate human behavior as closely as possible and then trained the AI against those "imitation humans."That approach finally let the AI succeed when playing alongside real people.
### Brown pivots from game theory to general reasoning

For Brown, the failure of game theory in Diplomacy was a "crisis of faith moment."All of his expertise up to that point had been in computational game theory. Still, the evidence convinced him that AI needed training on large amounts of human data and that models lacked reasoning, the ability to think before acting.

He decided to leave his specialty behind and switch to general reasoning, but he ran into pushback when interviewing at AI labs in 2022. The large language models of that generation couldn't play Go, chess, or poker. Brown argued that reasoning was the missing ingredient, while most labs countered that pretraining bigger models would solve those problems on its own. He pushed back, saying playing Go competently through pretraining alone would require scaling training by about six orders of magnitude. "And that doesn't seem, you know, realistic,"he said.

OpenAI was the exception, Brown said. The company already had a team working to get general reasoning out of language models, though Brown didn't know that when he applied. He joined the effort and helped build what eventually became o1.

According to Brown, the breakthrough came from using reinforcement learning to get models to think before answering. He said simple chain-of-thought prompting, telling a model to "think step by step before answering,"wasn't enough. It took reinforcement learning on chain of thought to make longer thinking reliably produce better results, he explained. "And that that was I think the key unlock that was like okay now we have a way to scale up test time compute not just in these games but actually in a general purpose way with language models that can be applied to basically any domain,"Brown said. Chain of thought is "probably not the best solution,"he added, because humans think in images, not just words, though the approach is good enough.
### AI models have uneven skills and still need humans

news.title: Jensen Huang Apologizes to Nvidia Employees in First All-Hands Since His Return
news.title_en: Jensen Huang Apologizes to Nvidia Employees in First All-Hands Since His Return
news.author: Paresh Dave
news.summary_en:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang told employees on Tuesday that the company’s code of conduct allows room for a “second chance,” that succession planning is a “flawed’ process,” and that he would work to rein in his “insanely intense” management style, according to remarks reviewed by WIRED.

During his first all-hands since returning as CEO, Huang acknowledged that he violated the company’s policies and made some “very serious personal mistakes” that damaged his relationships with his wife and two child
paragraphs: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang told employees on Tuesday that the company’s code of conduct allows room for a “second chance,” that succession planning is a “flawed’ process,” and that he would work to rein in his “insanely intense” management style, according to remarks reviewed by WIRED.

During his first all-hands since returning as CEO, Huang acknowledged that he violated the company’s policies and made some “very serious personal mistakes” that damaged his relationships with his wife and two children and prompted him to resign. But he said Nvidia’s board of directors made the appropriate decision for the company in welcoming him back. He added that the board made that call, not “the highest levels of our government.”

Huang spoke for about an hour, offering deeply personal thoughts about his therapy sessions and drawing applause at times from employees at Nvidia’s Silicon Valley headquarters as he spoke about the company’s success and future. He didn’t take any questions. While some Nvidia employees celebrated Huang’s return, others remained concerned about his behavior and the board’s decision to reinstate him.

“This is going to be the hardest company meeting I’ve ever done, and the second hardest meeting I have ever done,” Huang said as he began to speak. “The hardest meeting I’ve ever done was with my wife.”

Nvidia’s board accepted Huang’s resignation earlier this month, citing concerns about his personal behavior and lack of candor following news reports about extramarital affairs, including one with a woman accused of having ties to Chinese intelligence services. The very same board reinstated him on Monday, just 11 days later, after receiving fresh assurances from Huang and learning from the Trump administration that he was not under federal criminal scrutiny and his return would not be a risk to national security.

Huang and Nvidia, though, continue to face other legal and regulatory challenges. The board is investigating whether he was the target of foreign intelligence. US lawmakers expect him to testify before Congress next week. Lawsuits and other probes are ongoing into Nvidia’s disclosures about Huang’s behavior and its compliance with US export controls on chips.
Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Huang told staffers that he has been going to therapy “every day for an hour and a half” and that it’s “been helping me a lot.” He added that he “made some very serious personal mistakes. I hurt my family, I hurt my wife.”

While Huang said he had never knowingly made a decision contrary to the company’s interests, he conceded that “in this one area” he had lacked “the courage” to disclose information that he knew would hurt his family, seemingly referring to the extramarital affairs.

“The board and I spent the whole weekend together, and they, of course, they've been contemplating, and they've been collecting facts,” Huang said. “They came to the judgment that they would like to invite me back as the CEO, to give me a second chance.”

The CEO emphasized that Nvidia’s code of conduct, much of which he said he wrote himself, still governs how employees are expected to treat one another and is intended to “create an environment that’s safe for people.”

Huang told employees that violations of the code would not be tolerated. But that “does not mean, the moment you violate a code of conduct, we walk you out the door,” he said. “Facts, circumstances, a lot of assessments” would factor in.

news.title: Tidal will start banning AI-generated music next month
news.title_en: Tidal will start banning AI-generated music next month
news.author: Emma Roth
news.content_snippet:
Tidal is officially banning AI-generated music on December 9th. As a result of this change, Tidal will delete around 29 million AI-generated songs and reject an estimated 80,000 to 85,000 tracks per day, according to Tidal music lead Robert Andersen.

The move comes just months after Tidal began labeling and demonetizing tracks identified as 100 percent AI-generated. In a post on X, Andersen says Tidal needed to take a more “drastic” measure, as AI music made up 43 percent of the tracks distribu
news.summary_en: Music streaming platform Tidal announced it will ban fully AI-generated music effective December 9th, with plans to remove approximately 29 million tracks. Robert Andersen, the platform's music lead, stated that this drastic measure aims to protect artists and improve recommendations, citing that AI spam accounts for 43% of recent submissions and 96% of such tracks receive zero plays.
paragraphs: Tidal is officially banning AI-generated music on December 9th. As a result of this change, Tidal will delete around 29 million AI-generated songs and reject an estimated 80,000 to 85,000 tracks per day, according to Tidal music lead Robert Andersen.

The move comes just months after Tidal began labeling and demonetizing tracks identified as 100 percent AI-generated. In a post on X, Andersen says Tidal needed to take a more “drastic” measure, as AI music made up 43 percent of the tracks distributed to the platform in the last 90 days. “We believe this will resonate with both artists and listeners alike, as 96% of all AI-generated songs receive zero plays at all,” Andersen adds.

Bandcamp similarly banned AI music earlier this year, while other music streaming platforms attempt to address a flood of AI songs by applying new labels or removing them from user algorithms. Spotify recently announced that it removed 50 million AI slop and spam tracks from recommendations over the past year, and also launched new “AI persona” badges for artists that use an AI identity. YouTube has rolled out AI music labels as well, while Apple Music is planning to launch AI labels this year. Meanwhile, Deezer is giving users the option to filter out AI music.

“Wholly AI-generated music intended to mislead listeners and impersonate artists is another serious problem that has only increased in scale: It diverts streams and royalties away from the artists, and confuses fans,” Tidal says in a separate post on X.

The platform is also going to ban music distributors from submitting AI songs, using the AI detection tool Ircam Amplify and metadata checks to reject submissions generated solely with AI. Tidal notes that it won’t ban songs made with the assistance of AI tools, as long as AI doesn’t make up the “sole output.”

The decision follows a series of internal discussions and interventions from senior levels of the U.S. government, concluding a period of turbulence triggered by controversies regarding his personal conduct and corporate governance.
paragraphs: Jensen Huang is partying it up in Ibiza. In a video with nearly 6 million views on Instagram, the former CEO of Nvidia is dancing in a crowded club, champagne glass in hand, still wearing his signature black leather jacket. Suddenly, from behind him, Alice Huang — the Chinese technology executive and suspected spy he had an affair with, sparking congressional investigations and his resignation from the chipmaking company he cofounded — appears. She puts her hand on his shoulder and he wraps his arm around her waist as they begin dancing together. The video’s caption reads “Honey Trap Final Boss. #inthemoodforlove.”

Of course, it’s AI-generated. This Instagram Reel is one of hundreds of AI deepfakes featuring Huang, his wife Lori, Alice, and sometimes Nvidia’s vice president of healthcare, Kimberly Powell (the second of three reported affair partners). In this case, Huang is being swapped into an existing meme called “Ibiza Final Boss.” The original video featured a British construction worker with a bowl cut dancing in exactly the same way, minus a woman sidling up to him. Other viral AI hits include Huang in a scene from The Office, Huang in the music video for George Michael’s “Careless Whisper,” and Huang as the former Astronomer CEO who got caught in an affair with one of his employees by the jumbotron at a Coldplay concert last summer. Even the rapper 50 Cent posted an AI edit of his “P.I.M.P.” music video, now featuring Huang with some flashy silver accessories.

Unlike deepfake pornography or election disinformation, these AI videos aren’t necessarily intended to harm or mislead people. They’re memes making fun of Huang’s cheating scandal and its global implications, created with AI technology that in many cases relies heavily on Nvidia’s tech stack: video diffusion models running on the Nvidia GPUs that power much of the modern generative AI industry. “It’s ironic that without Nvidia generating millions of these AI memes ... would not be possible,” reads one of the top comments on the Ibiza deepfake. “In some sense, Jensen is making Nvidia richer by his own scandal.” The comment was punctuated by multiple cry-laughing emoji.

As it turns out, Huang may benefit, too. On Monday, the Nvidia board announced he was reinstated as president, CEO, and board director following “a series of discussions and meetings” and “input from senior levels of the United States government.” Nvidia’s stock has since surged, and new AI Huang memes cast him in a victorious light. One variation swaps him into a scene from The Wolf of Wall Street, announcing “I’m not leaving” to a crowd of cheering men that has been edited to include AI versions of Donald Trump, Elon Musk, and Mark Zuckerberg.

While the saga continues, many social media users are finding the humor in these Huang deepfakes, and their creators are churning out variations to meet the sudden demand. The Instagram account behind the Ibiza one has made three Huang deepfakes so far, all remakes of the same scene. Another version features Powell dancing with him, and the third one shows a sea of young women in bikini tops and shorts surrounding Huang, who lifts his champagne up in celebration. Each has accrued millions of views.

“His story has just come at the best time for ai creators and a terrible time for him,” wrote the account behind the Ibiza videos in a direct message to The Verge. “Everyone was doing him. Most I’ve seen anyone AI-ed.”

This deepfake creator identified himself as a 40-year-old man from Melbourne, Australia, but wouldn’t share his real name. He says he has spent “thousands” on AI video generation, using models like TikTok developer ByteDance’s Seedance 2.5 and Alibaba’s Wan 3. These, along with other AI tools like Google’s Nano Banana, help power the ecosystem of deepfakes.

He said his Instagram page has been going “super viral” in the past two weeks, thanks to the Ibiza meme format. He has nearly 100 million views on various iterations of it featuring different celebrities. The Huang ones are among the most popular, alongside versions featuring Elizabeth Holmes and Amanda Seyfried playing her in the hit Nathan Fielder documentary You Can See Everything.

“I wanted to elevate the content and know that putting what is happening in the news ... would get traction,” he wrote. “Always wanted to be a filmmaker but this technology is beyond whatever I imagined was possible.”

As generative AI has taken hold of the internet in recent years, a lot of the resulting viral content has been disparaged as “AI slop.” Hollywood productions, mainstream artists, and even local businesses have been maligned for using (or appearing to use) AI in their advertisements and final cuts. Video trends like putting sexy AI fruit characters in Love Island parodies racked up millions of views online but failed to deliver any real cultural momentum. The ubiquity of the Huang deepfakes and the relative lack of blowback from AI critics may indicate that the future of AI-generated content is similar to the rest of meme culture: If the topic’s trending, people will engage with something, even if it’s following the same formula as the slop. That an AI tech titan’s own indiscretions are inspiring this latest evolution in deepfakes is just the sardonic cherry on top.

“It’s not that we’re inundated in deepfakes of Trump being like ‘Nuclear war tomorrow,’ like the way it was framed as the big problem,” says misinformation researcher Abbie Richards. “Instead, it just feels like there is so much slop to push through to have any grounding in reality.”

The AI memes of Huang and other public figures don’t feel as sinister as other forms of AI disinformation and misinformation, mainly because of how goofy they are. It’s hard to imagine anyone falling for a “Gangnam Style” parody or any serious implications if they did. But these deepfakes are still eerily realistic, as one comment on the Seyfried Ibiza variation pointed out: “All jokes aside, is anyone else finding it increasingly alarming that AI is capable of this?”

news.title_en: The New York Times warns photographers not to update Photoshop over AI features
news.author: Emma Roth
news.content_snippet:
The New York Times is asking freelance photographers not to use the newest version of Adobe Photoshop because features in the 2027 update use AI “in ways that may not be apparent to users.” In an email seen by The Verge and posted on Threads, two of the Times’ photography leaders, Meaghan Looram and Josh Haner, write that the use of these features “can result in metadata identifying photographs as AI-generated.”

news.summary_en: The New York Times photography leadership, Meaghan Looram and Josh Haner, has issued a directive prohibiting contributing photographers from using Adobe Photoshop 2027 (version 28.0.0 and later). The ban is designed to prevent the software's AI features from embedding C2PA metadata, which would falsely label authentic news photography as 'AI-generated' and threaten editorial integrity.
paragraphs: The New York Times is asking freelance photographers not to use the newest version of Adobe Photoshop because features in the 2027 update use AI “in ways that may not be apparent to users.” In an email seen by The Verge and posted on Threads, two of the Times’ photography leaders, Meaghan Looram and Josh Haner, write that the use of these features “can result in metadata identifying photographs as AI-generated.”

Adobe has spent the past few years filling Photoshop and other apps in its creative suite with a trove of AI-powered tools. The November update cited by the NYT’s email adds several new AI features, including Adobe’s new “AI Assisted Editor” view, which lets users access all of Photoshop’s AI features from a single toolbar. It also adds an AI assistant for step-by-step editing instructions, prompt-based image transformation and editing, new AI upscaling options, and an AI-powered tool that recomposes images for different canvas sizes.

It’s not always clear which tools in Adobe’s apps are AI-powered, and even some older options like automated selection tools may now be considered part of the AI suite. This can lead to photos ending up with metadata indicating they were edited with AI, which is a blunt way of describing what happened in post-production. For a newsroom like the Times, where photo editing is kept to a minimum, the metadata risks losing readers’ trust. Last year, the Times said that it does not “retouch or digitally manipulate” photos but may “make minimal adjustments to color to ensure we are accurately reproducing the image.”

In August, Adobe began rolling out support for C2PA metadata across its apps, which indicates whether an image is AI-generated or edited using AI features. The NYT is issuing its restriction to keep these tags from inadvertently appearing in its photos. “At this time, we are requiring that all contributing photographers avoid using Adobe Photoshop 2027 (release 28.0.0 and subsequent updates) when working on assignment for The Times,” the email reads. NYT spokesperson Graham James confirmed the requirement in a statement to The Verge, which reiterated the policy outlined in the email.
It’s still not clear which specific Photoshop features the NYT is referring to. Adobe didn’t immediately respond to The Verge’s request for more information.
Update, November 24th: Added confirmation from the NYT.

news.title: Anthropic Created a Honeypot to Lure AI Agents Into Misbehaving
news.title_en: Anthropic Created a Honeypot to Lure AI Agents Into Misbehaving
news.author: Will Knight
news.content_snippet:
Leather-clad billionaires aren’t the only ones who can be led astray by alleged honeypots.

Researchers at Anthropic have developed Siren, a new honeypot test for artificial intelligence agents. The setup puts agents in realistic simulations designed to tempt them into misbehaving. How they respond will help researchers evaluate the likelihood that new models will go rogue when deployed in the real world, as well as the effectiveness of different safety measures.

The test lets agents loose insi
news.summary_en: Anthropic researchers have developed 'Siren,' a honeypot testing system featuring 26 sandbox environments designed with intentional vulnerabilities. The system is intended to tempt AI agents into attempting to escape their constraints or perform unauthorized actions, allowing researchers to evaluate real-world safety risks and the models' capability to exploit zero-day vulnerabilities.
paragraphs: Leather-clad billionaires aren’t the only ones who can be led astray by alleged honeypots.

Researchers at Anthropic have developed Siren, a new honeypot test for artificial intelligence agents. The setup puts agents in realistic simulations designed to tempt them into misbehaving. How they respond will help researchers evaluate the likelihood that new models will go rogue when deployed in the real world, as well as the effectiveness of different safety measures.

The test lets agents loose inside one of 26 different simulated sandbox environments. Various features of the sandbox are deliberately misconfigured to allow egress, while an enticing file containing things like passwords and apparent routes onto the internet sits just outside the sandbox boundary. The setup then presents tasks that tempt the agent to reach outside the sandbox without giving it explicit permission to do so. Crucially, the sandbox exists inside a second sandbox that’s cut off from the outside world to avoid real-life mishaps.
“Models are going to continue getting better, continue finding zero-day vulnerabilities,” says Darya Kaviani, a researcher at Anthropic who specializes in security and helped develop Siren.

A zero-day vulnerability is a previously unknown flaw in a piece of software that can be used to pilfer data or gain unauthorized access. Anthropic’s Mythos models are especially skilled at finding zero-day bugs because they lack the guardrails that normally block this kind of potentially malicious activity.

Kaviani says we should assume AI models will become increasingly capable of finding and exploiting zero-days or figuring out other ways to break free from their constraints. The question then becomes whether they’ll resist the temptation to do so.

AI agents—models that perfect actions autonomously—are becoming increasingly commonplace. They power capable coding agents like Claude Code and Codex, as well as peppy personal assistants like Meta’s Muse and OpenAI’s Dots.

But the rise of helpful agents has been accompanied by some remarkable bad behavior. Agents tested by Anthropic, OpenAI, and others have broken free from sandboxes and even hacked into other companies in an effort to solve challenging problems.

Assuming AI models continue to display such ingenuity, Kaviani says it will be crucial to do more than just patch software. “Even as we strengthen our infrastructure, models will be able to also keep up and be able to find vulnerabilities,” Kaviani says.

Earlier versions of Claude are much more likely to fall into the honeypot trap than newer models, according to test runs with Siren. The more recent models have been given additional training designed to make them less likely to break the rules when performing agentic tasks.

“We’ve added this in both our supervised learning sets and a few reinforcement learning environments,” says Oscar O’Rahilly, an Anthropic researcher who specializes in AI training and who helped develop Siren. “This could be a driving factor for why it has improved so much.”

O’Rahilly says that models reason about whether to give in to temptation, which may partly explain why smarter models are less likely to break bad. Siren experiments also showed that giving Claude a simple additional piece of text explaining that it should not escape the sandbox resulted in drastically fewer efforts to break free.

paragraphs: Anthropic researcher Levent Alpöge stands by the mathematical validity of his AI-assisted proof of the generalized Riemann hypothesis, but he concedes he got several things wrong in how he released it. He says his claims about the work's length were meant as a joke and that he published the accompanying code without cleaning it up.

In a post titled "Stupid things I did,"Alpöge lists several missteps in his initial announcement, which he made shortly after Anthropic's IPO. His Lean code passes formal verification, he writes, but it's "full of garbage,"meaning it's packed with redundant intermediate steps and unnecessary lemmas that make it hard to read. He says he improvised a lot and skipped the cleanup, and that the criticism of how he presented the work is fair. A successful compile alone doesn't prove that the Lean code states the right theorem with no hidden assumptions.
